analysis.one_liner: Caps power plant emissions of sulfur, nitrogen, mercury, and carbon dioxide through a national trading program.
analysis.headline: The bill never moved past its committee referral before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 — it received no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set national annual limits on four pollutants from large fossil-fuel power plants: sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and — for the first time ever — carbon dioxide, the main greenhouse gas. Plants would meet the limits by buying and selling emission allowances under a trading system, with new pollution limits phased in from 2008 through 2015. In exchange, it would give plant owners regulatory certainty and would relax some existing rules, including delaying stricter mercury standards and loosening requirements on plants that upgrade old equipment. It was a bipartisan compromise bill from Sen. Tom Carper, but it was introduced in mid-October 2002, less than three months before the Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near or downwind of coal- and oil-fired power plants, which produce about two-thirds of U.S. sulfur dioxide emissions and a third of the nation's nitrogen oxide, mercury, and carbon dioxide emissions [S3]. The bill's stated purposes include protecting public health by achieving substantial emission reductions and encouraging renewable energy [S3]. Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides cause acid rain, smog, and fine-particle pollution linked to asthma, heart disease, and premature death; mercury accumulates in fish and harms brain development in children. A carbon dioxide cap would have been the first national limit on power-plant greenhouse gas emissions. Renewable energy and nuclear units would also receive valuable emission allowances under the plan [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near and downwind of coal plants

how_it_helps.text: Sets national annual tonnage limits on sulfur dioxide from power plants, falling to 2.25 million tons by 2015 — far below then-current emissions — and on nitrogen oxides falling to 1.7 million tons by 2012 [S2] [S3].

Imposes the first-ever national cap on carbon dioxide from the electric generating sector, freezing emissions at 2001 levels from 2012 onward, with allowances also awarded to renewable and zero-carbon nuclear generation [S2] [S3].
Caps mercury emissions from coal-fired plants and requires maximum per-unit mercury reductions of 50 percent by 2008 and 30 percent of the mercury in delivered coal by 2012 [S2] [S3].

Requires plants to monitor and publicly report emissions of nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide quarterly, with fines of $5,000 per excess ton of nitrogen oxides, $10,000 per excess pound of mercury, and $100 per excess ton of carbon dioxide [S3].
Reserves portions of each pollutant's allowances for new units and new renewable energy units, so that new clean generation is not shut out of the market by incumbents [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners of coal- and oil-fired power plants, which would face new national emission caps requiring pollution controls, fuel switching, or the purchase of allowances. Some of that cost would likely flow to electricity customers through rates. The coal mining industry would face reduced demand as plants cut coal use or shift to cleaner fuels. In exchange, plant owners would gain regulatory certainty: the tonnage limits are locked in for 20 years before mandatory review, and the bill relaxes the new source review program, delays hazardous-air-pollutant mercury standards for covered plants by eight years, and exempts covered plants from certain visibility protection requirements for 20 years [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal- and oil-fired power plant owners

drawbacks.text: The bill substantially rolls back existing pollution rules to win industry support: from 2008 it narrows new source review so most upgrades at old plants escape full modern permitting, allows cost to limit required pollution-control technology, and exempts new plants in dirty-air areas from buying emission offsets [S3].

It shields covered plants from stricter mercury rules under the hazardous air pollutant program for eight years and from visibility protection requirements for 20 years — delaying protections that existing law would otherwise provide [S3].

The carbon dioxide cap is modest: the 2008 limit equals projected 2005 emissions, so emissions could still grow before the cap binds, and the tonnage limits cannot be revised by mandatory EPA review until 20 years after enactment [S3].

Allowance trading lets a plant keep polluting if it buys allowances, so local hot spots of sulfur, nitrogen, or mercury pollution near particular plants could persist even as national totals fall [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and environmental gains are large and real: deep cuts in the pollutants that cause acid rain, smog, fine-particle deaths, and mercury contamination, plus the first national carbon cap on power plants. The trade-offs are genuine but designed as bargains: relaxed new source review and delayed mercury and visibility rules give old plants room to operate longer, and the carbon cap starts loose. On balance, the bill delivers more to the public than it takes away, though a stricter bill could have captured the same emission reductions without the rollbacks — and its cap-and-trade design means some communities near heavy-emitting plants benefit less than national numbers suggest.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-October 2002 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which took no action on it before the Congress ended in early January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Thomas Carper introduced the Clean Air Planning Act of 2002 on October 17, 2002, joined by Republican Sen. Lincoln Chafee and Democratic Sens. John Breaux and Max Baucus [S3] [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S1] [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll call on the bill at any point before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1] [S5].
Only three senators cosponsored the bill — one Republican and two Democrats out of 49 senators in each party [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal- and oil-fired power plant owners and the coal industry are better off because the bill died: the first national carbon dioxide cap on power plants never took effect, and the stricter mercury, sulfur, and nitrogen limits were never imposed. Communities downwind of coal plants did not get the pollution reductions the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal-burning utilities and the coal industry

for.name: Sen. Thomas R. Carper
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 17, 2002, as a bipartisan multi-pollutant compromise covering sulfur, nitrogen, mercury, and carbon dioxide emissions from power plants.

for.name: Sen. Lincoln Chafee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Republican to do so.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 17, 2002, and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: George W. Bush administration
against.what_they_did: Promoted its own competing multi-pollutant power plant plan ('Clear Skies') that left out carbon dioxide limits, framing the debate around a proposal that did not include the carbon cap this bill contained.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew bipartisan sponsorship — a Democratic lead sponsor with one Republican and one additional Democratic cosponsor, out of 49 senators in each party — but it never reached a vote, so no party split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would impose deep national caps on the sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide these plants emit, forcing costly controls or fuel switching. But it would also hand them regulatory certainty locked in for 20 years, a relaxed new source review program, an eight-year delay of stricter mercury standards, and a 20-year visibility exemption — concessions that existing law did not provide.

Caps on sulfur, mercury, and carbon would push plants to burn less coal or wash and switch fuels, cutting demand for high-sulfur coal. The bill's own findings note the reductions would come largely from fossil-fuel-fired generation [S3].

The carbon dioxide trading program would award free allowances to renewable units and to nuclear generation above 1990 levels, giving zero-carbon sources a new revenue stream and a reserved allowance pool for new renewable units [S3].

industries.industry: Emission allowance markets and power trading
industries.note: The bill would build new trading systems for nitrogen oxide, mercury, and carbon dioxide allowances on top of the existing sulfur program, creating markets and brokerage activity. Trading lowers the total cost of compliance, which benefits electricity customers, but it also lets heavy local polluters buy their way out of cutting emissions at the stack.
